description: Avicennia marina is a hardy mangrove that tolerates salty and exposed coastal conditions. It is commonly recognized by pencil-like breathing roots around the tree base.
physical_characteristics: Hardy tree or shrub with greyish bark
leaf_characteristics: Leaves are simple, opposite, thick, and may look greyish underneath because of salt-management adaptations.
root_characteristics: Pneumatophores rise from waterlogged mud to help roots exchange gases.
ecological_importance: Reduces wave energy and shoreline erosion
Provides nursery habitat for fish, crabs, and shrimp
Stores blue carbon in roots and soil
history: Mangroves were known and used by coastal communities for centuries before formal scientific study. Coastal people valued them for fishing grounds, shoreline shelter, fuelwood, medicine, and navigation.
scientific_study: Avicennia species are studied for salt tolerance, pneumatophore gas exchange, coastal zonation, restoration suitability, and blue-carbon storage. Mangroves were documented by many botanists and ecologists rather than discovered by one person.
conservation_information: Avoid clearing mangroves for poorly planned coastal development
Prevent plastic, wastewater, and chemical pollution
Use native species and monitor survival in restoration
Record species, GPS, photos, and measurements for monitoring
interesting_facts: Pneumatophores act like breathing structures above the mud
This species can tolerate high salinity
Its roots help trap sediment along shorelines
references: Tomlinson, P. B. The Botany of Mangroves
Spalding, Kainuma, and Collins. World Atlas of Mangroves
FAO mangrove conservation and restoration guidance
conservation_note: Mangroves support biodiversity, coastal protection, and climate resilience.

root_characteristics: Breathing roots help oxygen exchange where sediment is waterlogged.

Stores carbon in coastal wetland soil

leaf_characteristics: Leaves are opposite, leathery, glossy green, and usually pointed at the tip.

ecological_importance: Protects coasts by slowing waves and trapping sediment
Helps reduce erosion along muddy shorelines
Creates nursery habitat for fish, crabs, and shrimp
Stores blue carbon in wood, roots, and waterlogged soil

scientific_study: Rhizophora apiculata is studied for stilt-root mechanics, propagule dispersal, taxonomy, coastal protection, restoration performance, and carbon storage.
